**@LordofTheMorning** (👍2 · 2016-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HbDeoPJ6sPc&lc=UgiH-761ZJK2yXgCoAEC
  Mostly good whilst you mentioned some of the differences between countries some of the differences whilst slight are rather important. I know about the way things work in the UK specifically Scotland but also the UK as a larger whole.
   
  Firstly you can be stopped by the police and whilst they must tell you why you are being stopped if you are not under arrest you can not just walk away. There are multiple powers in place that allow the Police to detain you to perform certain actions without being arrested or until you meet certain criteria. (Being detained as a suspect for questioning, Being detained under reasonable suspicion for search, Being stopped in a car, Being required to give some personal info if the police believe you are a witness or have information regarding a crime, or to detain you for your personal safety.)
  
  Secondly You are usually arrested before you are charged. Actually you will usually be officially charged upon being released from being arrested if your crime does not require an immediate court hearing, or at some point between being arrested and going to court if your crime is deemed sufficient to send you to court the next working day. All a charge is, is an official statement from the authorities to an individual that the court will be performing legal action against them for a crime they believe them to have committed. This is not required for an arrest. In most of the UK you can be "arrested on suspicion" of something which is to take you into custody to perform investigation. (In Scotland you will be detained for investigation (mostly a point of semantics but am important one), held for a maximum of 6 hours at which point you will either be released or then arrested, charged and either released or held for court the next working day.)
  
  This was a really good video, but I felt the need to clarify a couple of things due to the way things work in Scotland and the UK as a whole. Whilst the differences are small if someone from the UK was to watch this and try their luck and try say just walk away from an officer who has a legal right to keep them where they are, things are liable to go a lot less conveniently for that individual than they otherwise would and perhaps land them in some hot water they otherwise would have avoided.

  Pulled over in the US:
  1: Pull over in a well lit spot where there is room. Do Not get out of your vehicle unless the officer tells you to. 
  2: Turn off the engine and the stereo . Start recording audio.
  3:  Have your license, registration,  and proof of insurance ready with the window down when the officer walks up to your car. 
  4: Keep your hands visible.
  5: Be polite. Cooperate without talking too much.
  6: Never verbally consent to a search ,but don't try to physically stop a search even if it's illegal . 
  7: Do Not Resist arrest even if you didn't do anything wrong.

  I want to mention a gross error you made. Just because you are not under arrest does not mean you are free to go. There is something known in law as "Legal Detention" where YOU may not be under arrest, however you are not legally fee to leave and escaping this lawful custody is a crime. 
  E.G. The police stop you for speeding (or another traffic offense). You are unlikely to be arrested, however you are legally required to stop and produce documents such as a Driver's License and insurance. If you fail to stop for the police or leave before you are released, you can be charged with such crime. This is known as Legal Detention.  Further, the law usually requires that upon arrest and/or detention you are informed of the reason thereof.  
  Another example is if the police are investigating a crime-they have enough evidence to legally detain you for such investigation.

**@PauloSantosPHDS** (👍0 · 2015-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SS1HXcroEvE&lc=UgiZ9BoT_u7tzngCoAEC
  JamesESL English Lessons (engVid) Hello, Mr. James and Mr. E. (I'm your fan James' [tipsy] buddy... hehe). My name is Paulo and I am studying English (and hopefully learning it well). By the way, thank you so much Mr. James for all your hard work - your videos are fantastic. I am from Brazil, so my native language is Portuguese (Brazilians do not speak Spanish as a second language, most of them do not know Spanish at all. Actually, some Brazilians can understand Spanish because it is quite close, but not enough to speak the language).
  
  In Portuguese, specially in Brazil, there are two words that got different meanings (in a formal way), but Brazilians used to use them in the same situations. I am talking about the words "estudante" and "aluno." The "estudante" is the person who studies the content of a class (in the classroom or at home or anywhere else): student. The "aluno" is the person that only attend school, but it does not actually mean that that person is studying what he/she is listening to or writing about or watching in the classroom (the mind is far away, only the body remains in the classroom). Some people used to say: "Don't be an "aluno", be a student. When you get home, review your notes."
  
  My question is: Do Americans have a word for those people that are only in the classroom (students that do not read or memorize things but only attend school - sometimes for fun)? Brazilians used to translate "estudante" and "aluno" equally to the word "studant." Maybe I could say that better like this:
  
  Don't be an observer, be a student. When you get home, review your notes.
  Don't be a scholar, be a student. When you get home, review your notes.
  Don't be a schoolchild, be a student. When you get home, review your notes.
  Don't be a kid, be a student. When you get home, review your notes.
  
  However, this video clarified my mind and I started to think that that sentence could be expressed this way too: "Don't be a student, be a learner." (Still not the same thing, but I think it sounds good... hehe) 
  
  Thank you for your time and patience! I really appreciate it!
  
  Regards,
  ~ Paulo

  I'm a 20 year old native english speaker born and raised in the united states.
  I realized I didn't know this very clearly while learning a second language. 
  
  From my perspective 'this" is always acceptable.
  "that" is acceptable for almost everything 
  "that" can't be used if the object is in your hand
  but can be used if you hold more than one object in your hand
  
  
  If I hold only a single pen I can only call it "this pen"
  or i can say "that pen" if im a pissed off evil rich stepfather from a movie that spent $500 on a pen that my stepson just broke
  If I hold a pen and a pencil I can point and ask any of the following: "that or that?", "this or that?", "that or this", "this or this?"
  
  His explanation is good, but it's not very rigid. As long as you don't use "that" to talk about something relatively close and in the same sentence use "this" to talk about something relatively far away. Even that can be okay if you point clearly.

  Hi. Which is correct? Why? Thanks a lot.
  This is my mother and father
  These are my mother and father
    ↳ **@Annelisa8520** (👍0 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tZwOF0UHzsM&lc=UgyLRGZcbsZ-AXyF7y54AaABAg.9ltmuFNX1jLA2sb-_7N6hf
      Oh my goodness, English is weird  “This is my mother and father“ is correct, even though your mother and father are two people, and “these” is the plural. 
      
      As someone who has studied linguistics and speech-language pathology, I’ll take an educated stab at the reason! 
      
      You would correctly say “these are my parents,” because the word “parents” is plural.
      
      The words “mother” and “father” are both singular, and I think that first “this” is doing double duty—instead of saying, “this is my mother, and this is my father.”
      
      I think it’s one of those idiomatic English quirks that you just have to memorize because the rules don’t quite cover it.

    ↳ **@Butterposa2** (👍2 · 2017-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ef5zvdQwRLw&lc=UgjWF2ymORGLWXgCoAEC.88vcmiYHbDu8K4a_snWFRK
      The sounds are the same.  The only difference is that for the /th/ as in "this," you need to vibrate your vocal chords.  Compare this to the /s/ and /z/ sounds.  They are exactly the same.  The mouth position does not change.  The only difference is the vibration of the vocal chords.  Well, the same is true for the /th/ as in "this" and the /th/ as in "think."  "This" requires vibration, but "think" does not.  The mouth/tongue position does not change.  It is the same.  I hope this helps.

      @rainierjacobs  Absolutely that's more than enough. I "prepped" for 3 days, prepped as in watching some videos on youtube, doing some practice tests, etc. And I managed to get a overall 8 with 9 in lis, 8 in reading, 8.5 in speaking, 6.5 in writing. I was very nervous cause of the amount of posts made by people stating how hard IELTS is but from personal experience if you truly are fluent as you say you are, you won't have much problem with it. Some tips would be to watch some videos on how to manage your time in Reading since that's what most people struggle with. Also I would recommend you to take the test in comp  if you're decent at typing as the comp test has alot of benefits like having a timer, being able to highlight stuff, etc. For Speaking, I noticed that the questions the examiner asks aren't already chosen so I would advise you to try to lead the conversation into a topic you're more comfortable with. For example I was able to bring up AI as a topic and the examiner asked me more questions on that topic. And for writing, as you can see my score is horrendous. Unless you're going for a high overall score like 8.5 or 9, a score like 6 won't be a big issue since you'll be able to get enough from the other parts. Listening part was very easy (maybe I was lucky, I've heard the difficulty ranges from day to day so just pray)
      
      GOOD LUCK!

  Band 8.0 Speaking is where the feedback gets really nuanced — the examiner is looking for near-perfect fluency with only very occasional lapses. What this test demonstrates is that 8.0 candidates have completely internalised the band descriptors — their answers are extended without prompting, their vocabulary is precise and varied, and their grammar is almost entirely accurate. The feedback at this level focuses on micro-improvements rather than fundamental issues, which is actually encouraging for candidates at 7.0 — the gap is smaller than it appears.

  Sure, I can provide an example response to that question. If I were answering the IELTS question about the pros and cons of taking photos while traveling, it might go something like this:
  
  "On one hand, capturing photos during travels offers a tangible reminder of the experiences. It's a way to preserve memories and share the beauty of different places with others who weren't there. However, on the flip side, there's a risk of becoming too focused on photographing moments rather than fully immersing in them. Sometimes, in the pursuit of the perfect shot, one might miss out on the essence of the experience – the smells, the sounds, the subtle nuances of the environment. It's about finding a balance between documenting the journey and being truly present in it. Ideally, one should aim to create memories with their eyes and hearts first, and use the camera as a secondary tool to capture the essence of those memories."

  I attempted all questions correctly except altogether/ all together. Could you clarify the difference between altogether/all together in brief?
    ↳ **@ETBeducation [channel author]** (👍0 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zxpbCauwQP4&lc=Ugyo3OeerMzJEg4JwRl4AaABAg.9dKnyHWkb1_AAs8PXX1nHG
      Great question, Nabin! 😊 The difference between altogether and all together can be a bit tricky.
      
      Altogether is an adverb meaning completely or in total. For example: The trip was altogether wonderful.
      All together is a phrase meaning everyone or everything in one place. For example: The team was all together at the meeting.
      I hope that clears it up! Keep up the great work! 👍

## Learn English Grammar: Modals - "could" or "should"? — ENGLISH with James · engVid
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kLIQNJGwr44
- Video ID: kLIQNJGwr44
- Views: 512 199 · comments total: 224 · engagement: 0.44 comments/1k views

**@diego4493115** (👍80 · 2015-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kLIQNJGwr44&lc=Ugg5SeUai33qrXgCoAEC

    ↳ **@pmAdministrator** (👍0 · 2018-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kLIQNJGwr44&lc=Ugg5SeUai33qrXgCoAEC.7-H0Z7-JKjo8Wo7IMJ3qnM
      Best teacher that YOU'VE EVER SEEN?
      That seem to have something to do with his looks.
      Women...

**@fr6836-x1i** (👍3 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kLIQNJGwr44&lc=Ugx3JhoJZI_sKTYH5vx4AaABAg
  Could is used for 
  1)past capability- i could run 20 miles when i was young
  2) request/permission (may and can are bad for this) - could you suggest a good brand of phone?
  3) possibility (you can also use may/might) : he could/may/might make a full recovery one day
  
  
  Should is used generally for giving suggestions. However, would can also be used
  1)you SHOULD drink 3 litres of water everyday
  2) I WOULD suggest drinking 3 litres of water everyday

**@paulinho543** (👍5 · 2014-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=alg7qHta0Sk&lc=UggRDXde1QYl93gCoAEC
  To my mind, the right thing to do is not to think if the word is large or short. If the word ends with a sequence of "consonant", "vowel" and "consonant" (CVC pattern), we have to double the last consonant and add ING or ED in the end. For example:
  
  Rub (Consonant/vowel/Consonant) = rubbed
  Sit (Consonant/vowel/Consonant) = Sitting
  Stop (Consonant/vowel/Consonant) = Stopping
  
  But, like everything in life, there are exceptions. For instance, in words with two syllables if the stress is on the first syllable, we do not have to double the last consonant, even if the word ends with a CVC pattern. For example:
  
  Visit (CVC pattern, but the stress is on the first syllable 'vis') = visited
  Enter (CVC pattern, but the stress is on the first syllable 'en') = entering
  
  Simple as that.
  
  And yes, we Brazilians have problems with the pronunciation of certain words that do not have a vowel in the end or the sound of it is silent.

  Pretty good lesson, I really enjoyed. And I have a question: what is the difference between sure and assure? I hope your answer. Thank you.
    ↳ **@tommytruth7595** (👍0 · 2017-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SbN7-4zcIb0&lc=UgjFWcNJQxnGSHgCoAEC.7-H0Z7-U3__8UtrQ9ZmEW5
      To assure is more like giving a person some confidence, a promise, a guarantee, to tell somebody positively:
      
      "I can assure you that this is the correct road to NY City."
      
      "Are you sure about that?"
      
      "Yes, I am sure."
      
      The person who is assuring the other that it is the correct road is telling the person that the road  is without a doubt the correct road to use.
      
      He is asked if he is positive about that.
      
      And he says that he is.

**@MsEnglishCoach** (👍0 · 2014-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ew39SSJgb9c&lc=Ugi4cDHuj51Py3gCoAEC
  James, I think mentioning grammar texts only may send the wrong message to English learners.  The best coursebooks in my opinion are those which teach and encourage the use of all the skills: Listening, Speaking (sample conversations,   discussion topics), Pronunciation, Reading and Grammar.  Most of the students who come to me for tutoring have had grammar lessons in school but still don't speak with confidence.  I use books like New Interchange and Passages, Top Notch and Summit, American English File etc.  The student books have audio files, videos and other supplementary materials.  With some students, I use books specific to test preparation, as you mentioned or phrasal verbs, idioms, their specific occupation etc.

**@SabLMPh** (👍1 · 2014-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pXEwNme1YNU&lc=Ugh0WMvVcd2Wi3gCoAEC
  In Colombian Spanish there's the same thing with the word brother. And it has many sides. Some religious people tend to call you "hermano", because they assume we're all God's children, so you don't get offended because you expect it.
  When "regular" people use it there are two intresting scenarios. 1) Some people say to you "MI hermano" (MY brother) and it sounds kind of friendly (some people don't like it, though). Ex: "Mi hermano, ¿tiene la hora?" (My brother, have you got the time?). Personally, I don't get offended.
  2) Conversely, when people say just "hermano" without the possessive it sounds rude. In fact, when you get mad at someone, you call him/her "hermano/hermana" to express your hostility. Ex: "¿Cuál es su problema, hermano?" (What's your problem, brother?) - "Hermano, ya le dije todo lo que sé, ¡no insista!" (Brother, I told you all I know, don't insist!)... It's totally agressive. Some people use it with no bad intention, but the agressive usage it has makes it a bad option.
  Anyways, many like you just don't like any "brother" addressing for the same reason "hey, we're not brothers!".

**@mesmith8347** (👍9 · 2015-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pXEwNme1YNU&lc=UggN2U5bZ46iy3gCoAEC
  Actually, the words sex and gender are not interchangeable, though I'm seeing this mistake more and more often these days.  Sex is male and female, man and women.  It's the biological stuff that is the same in every culture and throughout history. It refers to things related to reproduction: chromosomes, gonads, genitalia, hormones, and skeletal structure.
  
  Gender, on the other hand, is what each society calls masculine and feminine.   It is cultural and consists of the personality traits and stereotypical roles that society has divided in half and given the labels masculine and feminine.  It varies from culture to culture and has not been consistent throughout history.  Its traditional purpose was to emphasize and call attention to one's sex, not to define it in the first place.  After all, a woman who wears combat boots, swears, and drives a truck for a living is every bit of a woman as one who wears high heels, loves makeup, and works as a hairdresser; the two women merely have different personalities.
  
  Male or female is your sex, not your gender.  When forms ask for  your "gender" they are  unwittingly asking if you are "a masculine" or "a feminine".  One's driver's license specifies one's sex, not gender and we refer to same-sex marriage, not same-gender marriage, to cite two examples.
  
  I think it is important to be careful to keep the usage of these two words distinct, because to use them as if they were interchangeable tends to obfuscate the meanings of both words, which adds to confusion rather than to clarify things.

  Some see gender as a personal internal view of one's self. Those who's sex does not fit what gender they feel they are, claim having gender dysphoria, and by that they are trans gender.
  
  Others see gender as a visual and physiological representation of a particular sex. Be it in how someone or something looks to be like, and/or how someone or something behaves.
  
  Such as a drawing or sculpture of a women is not a women. But it can represent a women to those who see it. So even though many who see such may call it a women, it is only a woman by visual gender identifiers to the viewer.
  
  The same is true for behavioral actions. A person can have the behavior and/or vocal sound of a type of sex, even without being of that actual sex. Case in point, in some cartoons. What you see and hear is not always what you get. Bart Simpson for example. You see and hear a boy, but the voice acting is done by a women. So Bart is seen as a boy, by visual gender identifiers to the viewer only. There is no real boy playing as Bart.
  
  To me, a person's sex is their biological sex. We use words as he, she, him, her, male, female, man, women, to state a type of sex. Where as gender is more of a representation of a sex, in what is called masculine and feminine traits. Traits that when exposed to them, can make a person think of a type of sex, even if it is not that type of sex. Such as what a cross dresser may do to those who see them.
  
  Some however is not satisfied with that, and insist words as he, she, him, her, male, female, man, women are gender identifiers, and not sex identifiers. This creates the socially created paradox I speak of. For if what is used to identify a person's claimed inner personality, rather than body type, the use of those words loose it's meaning for what it is suppose to represent to those who are exposed to it when used.
  
  If I was to say, "I seen a man today." What comes to mind? A person with boobs, and a vag? Or a person who is typically broad chested, and has a cock and balls?

If a man or a woman can be born to have natural boobs and a vag, or a cock and balls, how do we gain a concept of what a man and boy or a women and girl is, both physically and socially?
  
  To me, we no longer do. It becomes a paradox, with no real meaning. Sadly, this is today's norm, being forced on people to think like as what is true to think.
  
  What has become an issue do to this, has it's consequences. That being such arguments as to when and were we should see a person's sex or a person's personally perceived gender as more important.   First thing you need to realize is that English is a language. 
  
  It is not a subject you can learn. 
  
  The reason why you are still not fluent in English is that you are thinking about it as an obstacle. 
  
  It's a language, just like your native one. 
  
  You need to stop studying it, and start using it. 
  
  Use it for something fun, interesting and useful. 
  
  Doing exercises in it is the best way to be an English learner forever. 
  
  Start using it.

  second, reading book. i was reading a book every night even the comic book. because you need to consider that one day u could study in english university and there are  numbers of assessment you have to finish. so reading book can help you organise the sentences and correct grammar. there is one important thing u you to know speaking is not equal to writing. they are both totally different. speaking is speaking. writing is just writing.

      刘奕君 There is never 'one way' of improving your English as a non-native speaker. I think the problem is that we've grouped everything together under the 'academic subject' umbrella and we're ignoring the fact that language is like a sport: practice  makes perfect, so practicing over and over is more valuable than reading 101 different books- though that will help you A LOT. My advice to anyone would be to just start listening to YouTube videos in native American or British English- that will normalise the process and will make the writing and reading much more effective for you.

      A very good tip (In my opinion the best) that I think a lot of people don't know, is called "listening". It consists in listening to the same audio a lot of times until you master it. Step by step, you start with the simplest ones until you can go a little further. And when you get to this point, there's a website that has subtitles in English for TV Shows, so you can start listening to even harder audios.
      I'm learning English on my own for like 8 months, and i can watch a regular movie with almost no problems.
      Aforementioned website: http://ororo.tv/en
      I suggest "Friends" to start with 'cause it's very easy.
      BTW, I'm Brazilian too.

  Be careful when choosing a dictionary. I will give you an example:
  
  Merriam-Webster is the worst choice of dictionary or reference point. Much of the information they give is contradictory to what all other dictionaries say as a simple check will show. Merriam-Webster is also a profit making corporation unlike other sources and educational press.
   
  Let's look at the definition of 'Socialism'. We will compare the  Merriam-Webster definition to the definition given in the Collins Dictionary, The Oxford dictionary, The Cambridge dictionary and Google.
   
   
  Google definition of socialism
  a political and economic theory of social organization which advocates that the means of production, distribution, and exchange should be owned or regulated by the community as a whole
   
  Collins dictionary definition
  an economic theory or system in which the means of production, distribution, and exchange are owned by the community collectively
   
  Oxford dictionary definition
  A political and economic theory of social organization which advocates that the means of production, distribution, and exchange should be owned or regulated by the community as a whole
   
  Cambridge dictionary definition
  The set of beliefs that states that all people are equal and should share equally in a country's money, or the political systems based on these beliefs
   
  Merriam-Webster
  a way of organizing a society in which major industries are owned and controlled by the government rather than by individual people and companies
   
   As you can see, the Merriam Webster definition is the total opposite of all other sources. They are a profit making organisation, not an educational press.

      +JT it is not so difficult. The soft sign merely makes the letter more soft. Constants sound more like vowels, but not completely like them. The soft sign plays very important role in Russian because the great number of words will have different meanings with or without the soft sign. For example we have a word "мать" - mother and word "мат" - mat (also word "мат" have second meaning - offenseve, swear or "dirty" words). There is thousand of such examples.
    ↳ **@veronikatender9892** (👍0 · 2018-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3VtPci-R93E&lc=Ughq-Lr4KIs2u3gCoAEC.7-H0Z7-Gk4g8Zsw1AKyRrd
      while using "ь" with verbs, the difference is just in showing an infinitive form of verb. 
      For instance, compare: "I wanted it" - "Я хотел это" 
      and "I wanted to buy it" (where "to buy" is an infinitive) - "Я хотел купить это" (where "купить" is an infinitive)
      
      That's pretty easy :)
      And that was example why the grammar makes sense ))
    ↳ **@veronikatender9892** (👍0 · 2018-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3VtPci-R93E&lc=Ughq-Lr4KIs2u3gCoAEC.7-H0Z7-Gk4g8ZswJXJiNE4
      note that you can't say infinitive with a pronoun or noun (the same as in English). So you should use induce verbs.
      For example: он сказал (not "он сказать")
      она сказала (not "она сказать") etc.

      I think your opinion is an example of ‘badly expressed right idea’. I don’t think there is anything wrong with the American English: it’s just a variation of English like the Aussie English, Malaysian English, Indian English... u know wherever the British Empire was able conquer and left the legacy of using English as a primary language. There is also nothing wrong with the American accent, I know a number of people who are American and speak proper English, that is on par with the so-called British standards. Yet, there is a problem: it’s the lack of education, especially linguistic education. Americans don’t learn grammar, certainly don’t pay attention to classic literature (u know the good stuff whether it is English Dickens or American Mark Twain or Indian Salman Rushdie). But the bigger problem is that they way they, Americans, change English ripple across the world because they dominate media. And if you are someone who is accustomed to a certain (proper) way of spelling or using certain words, this can be really irritating to u.       well, let me try to work it out. "set up my computer" means arrange my unorganized computer. the next one is a bit tricky "set my computer up". in grammatical perspective "set" would act as the transitive verb, and i assume the subject is omitted before the verb, namely "I". "My computer" would act as the direct object of the transitive verb and finally "up" would act as preposition. Thereby the sentence "I set my computer up" means i put my computer above. correct me if you seen it wrong or it ain't sound good. i can only guarantee you that my answer is correct if i was James.

      i swear anki is only good for cramming before an exam, it’s utterly useless for knowledge you wanna acquire for the long term. its system is solid as spaced out repetition does work but the weakness is in the “repetition” part. at one point you gather so many flash cards that you simply do not have enough time in a week to revise them all regularly and effectively and i’ve noticed that whatever you learn from flash cards you forget soon after you stop revising no matter how much time you spent drilling it in. not to mention that you get used to recognizing the specific kanji and words in the format of the flash card because your brain remembers it visually aka the user interface of the app also aids a lot in that recognition, also the fact that in the flashcard you see the term on its own or in example sentences you get used to, instead of learning to spot it even when it’s blended with many other characters. but if you only hear the word in conversation or witness it in an article it would be significantly more difficult to recognize it when it’s not in the exact same size and color of the flashcard you’re using, and when it’s surrounded and connected to many other terms. with languages our brains are used to learn words and characters upon witnessing it many times in different forms, situations and contexts, that way we attach actual contextual memories and meanings to it and you do ingrain it in your long term memory effectively.

**@cirnobyl9158** (👍17 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DRpg-s8G8pk&lc=UgwFlPpviZdiwS6HQeR4AaABAg
  Personally I find Anki quite helpful and Duolingo quite bad.
  
  I'm fluent in English, French, and Chinese, and learning Japanese (taking N1 this year). So whenever a friend does Duolingo in any of those 4 languages (sample size a dozen), I'm always disappointed in how little progress they make after months and years of Duolingo. Somehow the gamified system says they're doing great, they've got a long streak or whatever, but in terms of actually being able to digest information they've barely gotten anywhere relative to how much time has passed.
  
  Meanwhile I've never touched Duolingo because I witnessed what happened to my friends, and instead used the Anki 2000 kanji deck for Japanese and yeah it was a painful grind, I'm not gonna pretend like it was comfy. Especially those obscure N1 kanjis like 妨げる (to hinder) which you'll rarely encounter. But language learning is hard. The grind has to be done sooner or later. If you're gonna have to grind at some point, why not use Anki, which claims to make the grind as efficient as possible? Idk if it truly is the most efficient but it's definitely one of the more efficient ways. The grind has now paid off and I can translate Japanese games and comic into English.

  Kanji Study is one of my all time favorite apps. If you buy the complementary add-ons it becomes a complete powerhouse. You have different options to order Kanji based on what material you want to follow (like by JLPT level, by school grade level, by Kanji Kentei level, etc.).
  You can practice stroke order, have a very flexible and customizable quiz mode (there are many options to configure it), you have flashcards for learning and reviewing, you can learn about the origins of each kanji and how it evolved over time, you have graded readers with explanations, you can use it as a dictionary, you can also learn the kanas ( Hiragana and Katakana) and radicals there, you can use a SRS automatic form of study, etc.
  And the best of all, you only have to pay once for each thing (one time for the app and one time for each add-on) instead of the subscription model of most apps.
  For me, Kanji Study belongs to the S tier, not the C one. But I respect that this is a list based on your preferences and personal experiences.

  I think the best approach is to mix apps. I think it's fine to start in an app like Duolingo to get your feet wet. The very beginning of learning a new language is hard because there's nothing you can read. So an app can make it more rewarding and easier to learn. Then once you have a decent vocabulary after maybe 3-6 months, I'd swap to a graded reader instead like LinQ or Satori Reader (For Chinese, I use Du Chinese, which is very good imo). Then pair that with chat GPT for practicing and roleplaying dialog and asking any grammar or vocab questions you have. And for Chinese and Kanji, you can add Skritter, but ignore the definitions and only use it for the writing. So for me, I'm learning Chinese and I started with Duolingo. Then I stopped early on once my vocab was good enough to start reading somewhat comfortably in Du Chinese (actually it was very uncomfortable in the beginning, but I really wanted to start reading so I just made the jump). And I pair that with Skritter for writing and ChatGPT for occasional conversational practice and questions.

  I actually like the duolingo heart system.  I think that if I make 5 mistakes in such a short lesson I shouldn't be able to brute force it, and I notice that as I get lower on hearts I start thinking each question through a bit more thoroughly. I think it's a good way to match your pace to your learning level.  I don't really see it as a "punishment", and I don't get that mindset.  Literally the only time it bothers me is when I lose one because of a typo but, idk that's not a huge deal.
  
  I definitely like it better than the energy system they've been rolling out, because you only lose hearts on mistakes, but you lose energy even if you get the question right.  So while hearts kind of let you go at the pace you should probably be going at, energy more or less matches the pace of everyone, and it negatively impacts the people who were doing well while not really doing anything to help the people who were doing poorly.

  Regarding the use of Anki, it's not difficult. The best way is to use sentences related to the content you're studying. I usually make about 5 for each vocabulary or grammar point I study and add them to Anki.

  I think Anki is amazing, I would put it in S (MAYBE in A, but not below). In particular, the combination Youtube+Anki is super. Every time I hear a new word in German I put it on Anki, and the deck is not from German to English, because many times it happens that you can do it from the foreign language to yours but not the opposite, which is in general more difficult. Instead, if you can do native->foreign you can usually do also foreign->native). So given an English input I must figure out the correct solution in German.

      @MUMEN_R1D3R the entire point of my comment is that it doesn’t matter how exactly you use anki, but that the app uses a completely opposite approach to teaching terms than our brains use to learn. we learn languages through noticing their patterns in different situations and attaching memories of the situation we were in when we spot the term. we need to make associations to learn in enough depth to be able to then use that term comfortably on our own. anki makes your brain use visual recognition of the sole term without any live context and it also makes you constantly translate in your head instead of relying on intuition and associations which is the primary way we use language. it’s okayish if you use it to get you somewhat familiar to new terms and grammar patterns, but you will never truly get fluent in any language if anki or any other flash card system is what you use most in your learning journey.

    ↳ **@LittleCheekyGuy** (👍7 · 2017-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0lHCemUta1w&lc=Ugha0XNxg-9p3HgCoAEC.8K57KGyW6kG8LnccBpvp3d
      Spare is something that is extra. For example, Daniel could have spare clothes. This means that you have more of something. You can use this in a sentence like: 'I have spare clothes that you could wear'. It could be to help someone where you can provide them with something, or for no reason.
      
      Downtime means the extra time you have to relax, enjoy yourself or do something different. It is usually the time after school or work - like weekends. For example, you could say: "I dance in my downtime".
      
      Overall, you could say: "Would you like to dance in our downtime? I have spare shoes for you if you don't have some."

  thx😀 but since "merely" means either "just" or "only", on which occasions should we use "merely" instead of "only"/"just"?
    ↳ **@ivetterodriguez1994** (👍0 · 2020-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z1PauShJx8c&lc=Ugwdg_kmDB35UKY9Nw54AaABAg.8kJWlFHWWS694BazaIQOZx
      "Mere" or "merely" means "solely" or "only" typically implying that something is insignificant, trivial, or excusable. "Just" is the word you would hear the most in spoken language. Only is typically used less than "just" but is interchangeable for the most part.

      Ce sont des synonymes.  La différence entre les deux autres est plus importante.  "Remind" veut dire "rappeler" et se fait à quelqu'un d'autre (ex. "Remind me to pay the bill") . Remember" veut dire "se rappeler" et est fait par soi-même (ex. "I didn't remember to pay the bill").  Est-ce plus clair ?

  when do we use "I am remembering"?
    ↳ **@Anglaide** (👍0 · 2019-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kPT3IBoFIaA&lc=UgzbOb5T-RG0aKh5vSd4AaABAg.8qSvnxiugaU8rYXKBE5Iz0
      We don't.  "Remember" is a verb of the mind and is considered non-progressive, i.e. it cannot be in progress.  You either remember or you don't.  The only exception might be if you had amnesia and things were slowly coming back to you.  But even then it would sound weird.

  1) Don't think, just listen - You can't understand 2 conversations at once.
   2) Ask questions - Engage to be engaged.
   3) Home Practice - 
    a. No subtitles
    b. 2-3 sentences
    c. 10x - for beginners/ 3x 
    d. Then play sub
    e.  Write down sentences you hear to know what you're missing and then practice what you've missed.
   4) Close your eyes and listen.
    a. It will make easier to listen for you, because when you lose one sense (vision in our case), another one's getting better(hearing).
   5) Order to watch movies:
    a. For kids
    b. Stupid comedy
    c. Action Movies
    d. Drama
    e. Dark comedy

  Hi Jennifer, thanks for brilliant lessons you always make.
  I have two points that i would like to ask you about
  The first point is that there are many teachers on youtube  who advise us to learn the synonyms of any word we lean, but frankly i don't find this way useful, because sometimes synonyms of the word wouldn't always make sense, if we wanted to replace the word in use by its synonyms.
  I'm not talking about your way, which is definitely perfect.
  The second point is that i noticed that you put a hyphen between two words in order to make a compound adjective. To be honest with you, i watched a lot of videos about compound adjectives, but the idea isn't clear enough. I hope that you may make a lesson about compound adjectives, because your ways of teaching are always understandable, and i trust you a lot.
    ↳ **@Englishwithjennifer [channel author]** (👍2 · 2019-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3bJo2t8_dic&lc=Ugxiy4GruCFNc4IG-YR4AaABAg.8skY0Q8LTZE8ske91AJCSl
      Hi. If you're able to join the live stream on Monday, please do. I'll show examples of how to choose appropriate synonyms. See my reply to Haider above, too. You need to be very aware of associations a word has, and you need to pay attention to context. How do people use those synonyms? Think of the phrases I've given you:
      an intriguing question
      a thought-provoking story
      a creepy feeling
      hilarious scenes
      etc.
      Learning phrases will help more than memorizing single words. 
      
      Compound modifiers/adjectives usually require a hyphen when we use a present or past participle:
      the strangest-looking thing
      a thought-provoking story
      a time-honored tradition
      a well-built car
      
      This is a handout for teachers, but you may use it for self-study. :) https://englishwithjennifer.files.wordpress.com/2014/03/finding-four-leaf-clovers_handout1.pdf
      
      I'll note the request for a lesson on compound words/compound modifiers.

      +Matheus Mascarenhas The difference lies on what are you trying to say. If you saw a movie and have an opinion about it  'saw' explains it.   Side note: Too can also be used in another way. I'll explain with a sample dialogue.
  
  A: What is your favorite color?
  B: My favorite color is blue.
  A: Really? Me too!
   
  Character A is implying that blue is also their favorite color.
  Too sum up, "Too" can be the same as "also", but saying "me also" would sound very weird.

  Assume (casual usage)= “without tangible evidence, or to be reluctant and take the element of evidence for granted”. eg) take up position, expect, believe, think.
  Presume (formal usage)= “Based on previous evidence, because the evidence recurred in the past ”. eg) arrogant and overconfident presumptions or presupposed.

  The definition of "presume" that James gives in this video is incorrect. Presuming something doesn't mean that there is any prior evidence. The "pre-" part means "before", but it implies that you are taking something as given *before* taking into account any evidence. "Presumed innocent" means that you are treated as if you are innocent before the verdict is reached.

    ↳ **@danamonightbird2957** (👍0 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tg6zAkYRAH4&lc=Ugx1cpOVrXRuDOWKOHp4AaABAg.8Gc6v4rEj-L9s4oCwfYyv9
      There is no difference in meaning but it is more common to use "How long" it can sound less formal and many speakers find it more natural. "How much time" it is often used when asking about a shorter length of time. You might use "how much time" to ask for the amount of time it takes to cook something. And you might use how much time to ask for the estimated length of time it takes to do a task. For example:
      How much does it take to cook rice?
      How much time will it take to clean the house?

  is there any difference between: ''I did say'' or '' I said'' ?????
    ↳ **@danamonightbird2957** (👍0 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tg6zAkYRAH4&lc=UgyUks602yaR_J5UR8V4AaABAg.8Gbj9y8gNqy9s4iiihN9UR
      "I said" is standard. "I did say" is more insisting (we sometimes use do, dose, did, followed by the bare infinitive of the main verb to express emphasis).
      Example:
      A: [After a long conversation] Well, that's about it. 
      B: You said you'd tell me everything you knew about it. 
      A: I did tell you everything about it.

**@ВиталийСлонов-ч4ъ** (👍1 · 2017-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4wqI-UW1P0I&lc=Ugi2C8phj60T03gCoAEC
  Granted, unless we are talking about physical closeness, the adjective 'near' can be used like a preposition, with or without 'to'. E.g. I live near the station. 
  However, when we are *not talking about physical closeness, 'near to' is often preferred. E.g. I came very near to being offered the job. I was getting cold so I moved near to the fire. I was near to panic as I realized that I was trapped. People near to retirement need to know their pension funds are sufficient. They are near to solving the puzzle.
  The comparative and superlative 'nearer' and 'nearest' are generally used with 'to', though 'to' can be dropped in an informal style. E.g. Come and sit nearer (to) me. Who's the person sitting nearest (to) the door? 
  To sum up, we must sometimes distinguish between physical and figurative senses when it comes to using 'near', mustn't we? Concur?
  Thank you for the video, James.

  Love your vids, James!!  But don't forget other prepositional phrases with 'blow':  'Blowout' can mean a huge party, or a hairdo at a salon. ex., "Hey Sally!  Did you just get a blowout/get your hair blown out? - "Why, yes Patsy, I'm going to Zed's huge blowout in the barn tonight!"   Also, ' to blow over' can mean something strong which has recently subsided, as in a storm or an argument. And don't forget "blown away" meaning "really impressed", as in "I was blown away by James' English lesson"

**@lcozzarelli** (👍0 · 2014-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bwdhlrhziSA&lc=UgwbG923UEIe66wcbHx4AaABAg
  Also "to blow (someone/something) off" means to ignore a person/thing or to not show up for a planned meeting with that person, e.g., "Lydia was supposed to meet me at 7:45 for the 8pm show, but she blew me off."  (I think one would say "blew me out" in the UK, but it's "blew me off" in the US).  You can also blow things off, e.g.,  "I blew off my homework to go bike riding with Mark yesterday, but now I'm regretting it."

  Ten advanced words for ielts speaking to improve your score :
  1.Exacerbate (v).- to make something worse. 
  (Collocations- problem ,situation, impact, effect.) 
  2. Mitigate (v). - make less severe, less unpleasant. 
  (colloc.-problem, impact, effect, suffering) 
  3.Unsurmountable (adj.)- impossible to solve. 
  (colloc. -barrier, problem, challenge). 
  4.An uphill struggle - difficult /challenging but possible. 
  (colloc. -task, project, game). 
  5.Apprehensive (adj.) - worried or nervous about a bad result.
  (Colloc.-apprehensive about...)
  6.Disgruntled (adj.) - unhappy and disappointed /dissatisfied.
  7.Bewildered (adj.) - confused. 
  (colloc. - thoroughly, utterly, bewildered by...). 
  8.To do my utmost - to try my best. 
  9.Inept (adj.) - not good at your job /showing a lack of skill. 
  (colloc. -very, rather, totally, politically, socially, inept at) 
  10.Impeccable (adj.) - perfect without fault. 
  (colloc. - Job, behavior, manners, English)
  Enjoy learning...

  Exacerbate= make sth worse
  Mitigate= make less unpleasant 
  To do my upmost= try my best
  Disgruntled= unhappy, disappointed, dissatisfied 
  Bewildered= confused
  An uphill struggle= difficult problem but it doesn’t mean that cannot solve
  Unsurmountable= impossible to solve
  Tricky= difficult 
  Turn out, come out= finish 
  Impeccable= perfect
  Apprehensive = worried, scared abt a bad result
  Inept= not good at sth, showing a lack skill
  Laborious= difficult

**@DatNguyen-fr7oz** (👍0 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DxfQFioD3SA&lc=UgzfEoqzXvLXvJqXcnt4AaABAg
  ADVANCE VOCABULARIES FOR IELTS
  
  Ten advanced words for ielts speaking to improve your score :
  
  1.Exacerbate (v).- to make something worse. 
  (Collocations- problem ,situation, impact, effect.) 
  
  => THE PROBLEM OF CLIMATE CHANGE IS EXACERBATED BY PEOPLE FLYING TOO MUCH AND CREATING CARBON EMISSION
  
  2. Mitigate (v). - make less severe, less unpleasant. 
  (colloc.-problem, impact, effect, suffering) 
  
  => WE COULD MITIGATE THE IMPACT OF CLIMATE CHANGE BY FLYING LESS
  
  3.Unsurmountable (adj.)- impossible to solve. 
  (colloc. -barrier, problem, challenge). 
  
  => ALTHOUGH CLIMATE CHANGE IS A CHALLENGING PROBLEM, IT'S NOT UNSURMOUNTABLE TO SOLVE
  
  4.An uphill struggle - difficult /challenging but possible. 
  (colloc. -task, project, game). 
  
  => WRITING MY NEW BOOK HAS BEEN AN UPHILL STRUGGLE
  
  5.Apprehensive (adj.) - worried or nervous about a bad result.
  (Colloc.-apprehensive about...)
  
  => INITIALLY , I WAS REALLY APPREHENSIVE ABOUT MY DRIVING TEST, BUT IN THE END, IT TURNED OUT REALLY WELL
  
  6.Disgruntled (adj.) - unhappy and disappointed /dissatisfied.
  
  =>THE CUSTOMER SERVICE WAS HORRIBLE, I  FELT RATHER DISGRUNTLED
  
  7.Bewildered (adj.) - confused. 
  (colloc. - thoroughly, utterly, bewildered by...). 
  
  =>  I WAS UTTERLY BEWILDERED BY MY FRIEND'S DECISION TO QUIT HIS HIGH PAID JOB
  
  8.To do my utmost - to try my best. 
  
  => THE AUTHORITY HAVE PRODUCED A GOOD ECONOMIC PLAN AND I AM SURE THEY WILL DO THEIR UTMOST TO IMPLEMENT IT.
  
  9.Inept (adj.) - not good at your job /showing a lack of skill. 
  (colloc. -very, rather, totally, politically, socially, inept at) 
  
  
  => MY BOSS LIKES TO DESIGN HIS OWN PP, BUT BETWEEN YOU AND ME, HE'S RATHER INEPT AT IT.
  
  
  
  10.Impeccable (adj.) - perfect without fault. 
  (colloc. - Job, behavior, manners, English)
  
  => MY FRIEND LIVES IN AMERICA, AND SHE SPEAKS IMPECCABLE ENGLISH.
